mcqs.question: What makes the "one example threading through all five letters" answer stronger than "one example per letter"?
options: It proves you can recognize all five failure modes and fixes in the same piece of code, not just recite five isolated definitions
It is shorter to say out loud, which matters more than the content in a timed interview
It avoids using any code, which most interviewers prefer
It only requires memorizing one definition instead of five
mcqs.explanation: The threaded version demonstrates applied understanding — you show the same class getting worse and then fixed one principle at a time, which is exactly what an interviewer can't verify from five disconnected toy examples. It isn't about brevity, avoiding code, or memorizing less; you still need all five definitions, just applied consistently.

mcqs.question: In the fully-refactored `NotificationSender`, which detail demonstrates ISP specifically (as opposed to DIP or OCP)?
options: A new channel can be added as a new class with zero edits to `NotificationSender`
`NotificationSender` depends on the abstract `Channel` type rather than `EmailChannel`
The `Channel` interface exposes exactly one method, so no implementer is forced to support methods it doesn't use
mcqs.explanation: A single-method interface is the ISP signal — nobody implementing `Channel` is stuck providing unused methods. Constructor injection is the DI mechanism (supports DIP), adding a channel with zero edits is OCP, and depending on the abstract type is DIP itself — all real, but not what ISP specifically names.

mcqs.question: Splitting `Repository` into `Reader`, `Writer`, and `Deleter` satisfies ISP but most real callers depend on all three anyway. What's the right response to this tension?
options: Always split, since ISP is a stricter rule than API cohesion
Never split, since a cohesive API always beats interface segregation
Name the trade-off explicitly and decide based on how many callers actually use only a subset of the methods
Split the interface but make all three inherit from each other so callers don't notice
mcqs.explanation: Principles conflict sometimes, and the senior answer names the actual cost of each option and picks based on real caller behavior — if most callers need the whole surface, splitting adds ceremony without isolation benefit. Treating either principle as an absolute winner, or hiding the split behind inheritance, dodges the actual judgment call.

mcqs.question: A three-method utility class that never changes and has no variation points is left as one class, un-split by any of the five letters. Is this a SOLID violation?
options: Yes — every class must apply all five principles regardless of size or change frequency
No — the principles name failure modes to watch for; a class with none of those failure modes present gains nothing from being split further
Yes, but only if the class is in a public library rather than internal code
No, but only because utility classes are explicitly exempt from SOLID by convention
mcqs.explanation: SOLID principles describe smells to fix when present, not quotas to hit on every class — a small, stable utility with no real variation or multiple responsibilities has nothing to fix. There's no public/internal exemption rule and no blanket "apply all five everywhere" requirement; over-applying them to code that never varies just adds indirection.
